In addition to direct payments, Government is considering offsetting outstanding debts against royalties and taxes that electricity producers owe the state. Negotiations are also underway with state-owned oil company NNPC Ltd to lower the price of gas supplied to power plants.
Minister of Power Joseph Tegbe, said Nigeria expects to complete the repayment of outstanding debts to electricity producers in 2027, with more than a third of the negotiated amount already settled.
Speaking on television channel Arise News on November 23, the Minister said the government had paid 1.23 trillion naira ($883 million) to the companies concerned.
The total debt negotiated with producers was reduced to 3.3 trillion naira ($2.37 billion), down from an initial estimate of 6 trillion naira ($4.31 billion). The government intends to settle the remaining balance through a combination of payment mechanisms.
Tegbe described the proposed reduction as a way to ease producers’ operating costs over the longer term.
The measures address unpaid bills accumulated by power generation companies, known as GenCos, between February 2015 and March 2025. According to the Nigerian presidency, the repayment program approved by President Bola Tinubu in April 2026 covers verified debts from that period.
By then, 15 power plants had signed agreements covering a portion of their recognized claims. To finance the initial payments, the government reported that it had raised 501 billion naira ($360 million) through a first bond issue. A second bond issue worth 729 billion naira ($523 million) was completed in September. On October 9, Nigerian Bulk Electricity Trading (NBET) announced that payments under the second round of financing had begun.
To supplement direct payments, the government is exploring arrangements that would offset royalties owed by electricity producers against their outstanding claims on the state.
Tegbe also raised the possibility of similar arrangements involving corporate income tax. Both mechanisms remain under discussion with the companies concerned.
According to the minister, such arrangements would eliminate the need for the government to collect money from producers only to return it through debt repayments.
He also noted that public resources must be allocated across several sectors, including education, healthcare, and agriculture.
These competing budget demands are among the reasons the government is exploring alternatives to direct payments. Beyond the settlement of existing arrears, preventing the accumulation of new debt remains a major challenge.
In July, the Association of Power Generation Companies estimated that new arrears might exceed 7 trillion naira (approximately $5.02 billion) before the repayment program is completed.
Gencos Chief Executive, Joy Ogaji, said payments to electricity market participants remain insufficient.
